title: Design Hit Counter
statement:
Build a class `HitCounter` that records hits and reports how many of them happened recently. Time is measured in whole seconds.

- `HitCounter()` creates a counter with no hits recorded.
- `hit(timestamp)` records one hit at second `timestamp`. Several hits may share the same second.
- `getHits(timestamp)` returns how many recorded hits lie in the 5 minutes (300 seconds) that end at `timestamp`: the hits at a second `t` with `timestamp - 300 < t <= timestamp`.

Calls come in time order: the `timestamp` given to any call (of either method) is never smaller than the one given to the call before it.
constraints: Timestamps never decrease from one call to the next
At most 300 calls in total are made to hit and getHits
notes:
## Intuition

The simplest counter keeps every hit and, on each `getHits`, counts the ones inside the window: O(total hits) per query. Because calls arrive in time order, the stored hits are already sorted, and a hit that has fallen out of the window can never come back into it: later queries only move the window forward. So the hits form a queue: new hits join at the back, and expired ones leave from the front. The answer is simply the queue's length.

## Approach

1. Store hit times in `queue`, with `head` marking the oldest hit still in it (moving an index is O(1), unlike `Array.shift`).
2. `hit(timestamp)`: push `timestamp` onto the back.
3. `getHits(timestamp)`: while the front hit is at or before `timestamp - 300`, it is outside the window, so advance `head`.
4. Return `queue.length - head`, the number of hits that remain.

## Example 1, step by step

- `hit(1)`, `hit(2)`, `hit(3)` make `queue = [1, 2, 3]`, `head = 0`.
- `getHits(4)`: the cutoff is `4 - 300 = -296`; the front hit 1 is after it, so nothing leaves. Returns 3.
- `hit(300)`: `queue = [1, 2, 3, 300]`.
- `getHits(300)`: cutoff 0; nothing leaves. Returns 4.
- `getHits(301)`: cutoff 1; the front hit 1 is at the cutoff, so `head` becomes 1; hit 2 stays. Returns `4 - 1 = 3`.

The output is `[null, null, null, null, 3, null, 4, 3]`.

## Complexity

- Time: `hit` is O(1); `getHits` is amortized O(1), since each hit is passed by `head` at most once.
- Space: O(total hits). A follow-up variant keeps 300 buckets of (second, count) instead, which uses O(1) space even when one second has millions of hits.

## Pitfalls

- The window excludes its left edge: a hit at `timestamp - 300` no longer counts, so evict with `<=`, not `<`.
- Several hits can share a second; store each one (or a count), not one entry per second.
- `getHits` before any hit must return 0 without reading past the end of the queue.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `queue` | every hit time, in the order the hits arrived |
| `head` | index of the oldest hit still inside the window |
| `timestamp` | the current second given to the call |

narration.3: All hit times go into one array that is used as a queue.
narration.4: head points at the oldest hit that may still be inside the window.
narration.8: A new hit is always the newest, so it joins the back of the queue.
narration.12: While the oldest remaining hit is at or before timestamp - 300, it has left the 5-minute window.
narration.13: Drop it by moving head forward; it can never count again because time only moves on.
narration.15: Every hit from head to the end is inside the window, so the count is the queue's remaining length.
